editorial.headline: Managing Accommodation, Not Owning It
editorial.standfirst: This is the business of running accommodation for an owner—fully foreign-open nationally, yet unavailable for PMA registration in Bali today.
editorial.body:
Accommodation-management services occupy the space between ownership and advice. The activity is performed by a third-party manager that takes responsibility for an accommodation business’s overall commercial and operational performance. That responsibility is practical, not ornamental: it includes direct involvement in daily operations and managerial decision-making. The manager acts for the property owner and receives a management fee. Put plainly, this is a mandate to manage the operation, rather than to own and directly operate the accommodation property, or to provide general management advice without direct operational control.

The appropriate registrant is therefore the third-party manager acting for the owner, with a real operating role rather than a purely advisory one. The activity is open at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. Its defining feature is the degree of responsibility assumed by the manager: overall business and operational performance, day-to-day involvement, and managerial decisions made on the owner’s behalf. The final reference to hotel-management services confirms the practical character of the activity without changing that wider accommodation-management frame.

At the national level, this open activity permits foreign investment up to a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. That national position must not be mistaken for a Bali registration route. In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity today. The Bali status is blocked on risk classification: at the Besar scale, OSS risk across every scope is Low or Medium-Low, and the province’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA. The stated trigger is the Bali moratorium of May 2026. National openness remains the national position; Bali’s block is the local result for PMA registration.

That distinction matters because the formal subject here is a management service, not ownership of the property being managed. The national position reaches every listed business scale and permits full foreign ownership. Yet the Bali assessment resolves differently for PMA because of the stated risk-class rule, not because the national foreign-ownership ceiling is lower. For a founder considering a Bali base, the reading is uncompromising: national foreign openness describes the activity, while the island-wide moratorium prevents PMA registration there today.
